#996. Starbucks sales miss expectations, but its U.S. turnaround is gaining steam

Starbucks on Thursday reported mixed quarterly results as its international cafes underperformed expectations.

However, its U.S. turnaround continues to take hold, as its home market topped expectations during the coffee giant's final quarter of fiscal 2026.

"We enter fiscal 2027 with momentum, a clear set of priorities and higher ambitions for what Starbucks can become," CEO Brian Niccol said in a video shared on the company's website.

Starbucks is ahead of schedule to meet the fiscal 2028 targets laid out at its investor day in January, he said on the company's earnings conference call.

For fiscal 2027, Starbucks is projecting adjusted earnings per share in a range of $3.15 to $3.25, above Wall Street's expectations of earnings per share of $3.14. However, its anticipated revenue decline of 1% is weaker than expected; analysts were forecasting net sales growth of 1.4%.

Starbucks is projecting North American same-store sales growth of 4% for the fiscal year.

The company's earnings and revenue outlook includes an additional week and the effects of the shift in its China business to a joint venture business model. Starbucks is also projecting slight deflation in coffee prices and slowing net new North American cafe openings, which will both weigh on its full-year revenue, according to CFO Cathy Smith.

Here's what the company reported for the quarter ended Sept. 27 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Starbucks reported fiscal fourth-quarter net income attributable to the company of $677.2 million, or 59 cents per share, up from $133.1 million, or 12 cents per share, a year earlier.

Excluding restructuring and impairment costs and other items, the company reported earnings per share of 80 cents.

Net revenue fell 4% to $9.14 billion, reflecting the joint venture deal in China.

The company's global same-store sales increased 7.2%, fueled by growth in average ticket, and beating Wall Street estimates of 6%, according to StreetAccount. Transactions grew 1.8% in the quarter.

Starbucks' U.S. cafes reported same-store sales growth of 7.7%, topping StreetAccount estimates of a 6.5% increase.

Under Niccol's "Back to Starbucks" strategy, the company has focused on improving service, making its cafes more welcoming and sharpening its marketing. The changes have helped to win back customers.

"Starbucks brand affinity is at near record levels as our menu innovation, marketing and merchandise continue to create moments that drive culture and bring people into our coffee houses," Niccol told analysts.

The company said its North American rollout of its fall menu, which includes the iconic pumpkin spice latte, was the company's strongest ever autumn launch day. And matcha is now a $1 billion drink for Starbucks.

Outside of North America, the company's international comparable sales ticked up 0.9%, as traffic declines offset an increase to average ticket. That growth fell short of analyst estimates of a 3.2% increase, according to StreetAccount.

After its China business transitioned to a joint venture, Starbucks has shifted most of its international business to a licensed model, allowing local operators to take charge. The company is also exploring selling a majority stake in its Japan business, Reuters reported in September.

Starbucks opened 303 net new cafes during the quarter. In September, the company announced it would close about 1% of its North American footprint, or about 250 locations, as part of its turnaround.

By the end of its fiscal year, across the U.S. and Canada, the company also completed more than 1,700 cafe uplifts, meant to make its stores more welcoming to customers. The company has said locations that receive a makeover, with tweaks like increased seating and softer lighting, see higher transactions in the aftermath.

#994. Wagner brothers begin new NBA chapter on different paths

After five years, brothers Franz and Moritz Wagner are no longer playing together for the Orlando Magic. In the new NBA season, their separation will likely mean the new "German" team is the Charlotte Hornets.

In 2021, when Franz Wagner joined the Orlando Magic to start his NBA career, his older brother Moritz was already on the team. Franz, who is four years younger, was selected eighth overall in the draft by the team who had signed Moritz a few months earlier.

It's not just their joint appearances in the NBA that have since turned the "Wagners" into something of a brand in basketball. Just last year, the NBA had a regular-season game in Berlin, partly because of the Wagner brothers.

Moritz is a successful podcast host and often has his brother on the show. Both have their own Instagram accounts, each with around 300,000 followers. In 2024, the German public broadcaster ZDF aired a four-part TV documentary about the brothers, chronicling their basketball history and close relationship.

In recent years, they've also celebrated success with the German national team. In 2023, they became world champions together and were then at the Olympic Games in Paris a year later. In 2025, Franz also won the European Championship title, while Moritz, sidelined by injury, watched on as a TV analyst.

This summer, their time together came to an end. After Moritz wasn't offered a new contract in Orlando, he accepted an offer from the Brooklyn Nets. He now lives in New York with his girlfriend, Maggie McQuade, who works in marketing for the NBA.

"I've already spent a lot of time in New York. It's kind of like my home in America," Wagner said on his podcast, adding that it reminds him of where he's from. "As far as the US goes, Brooklyn is actually very close to Berlin."

The call from the Nets proved a stroke of luck. "When we hung up the phone and both agreed, we both cried. Because you kind of realize that this move feels right somehow," Wagner said. "We're just staying home."

The Nets are considered one of the weaker teams heading into the upcoming season, leaving Wagner a key force in providing stability and helping to develop younger players.

Franz is staying in Orlando. Alongside Paolo Banchero, Franz is one of the team's two stars. The 25-year-old is on a massive contract that runs through 2030 and will earn him a reported total of $224 million (€199 million).

With Sean Sweeney hired as their new head coach for the upcoming season, the Magic are hoping to finally advance past the first round of the playoffs, having lost at that stage in each of the last three seasons.

Success is expected to come from a faster style of basketball than has been played in Orlando in recent years. In the new system, Franz Wagner will take on the role of point guard more prominently than before — moving the ball up the court, creating his own shots, and driving to the basket with speed — much like he does for Germany.

"We want to play tough, play together, play it fast and enjoy playing together," Wagner said during a preseason interview. "We got a little bit more space for our guys, to get in the paint and make plays, for themselves and for others."

However, he now has to manage without his older brother.

"I think we're both a little sad his time here has come to an end," Franz Wagner said in an interview with sports news site ClutchPoints. "I think, though, we're both really grateful for the time we had [together]. To play with a sibling in the NBA for so many years is super special. So we're just grateful for that."

Now that the Wagners’ time together in Orlando is history, German basketball fans may have to adjust their allegiances a bit for the upcoming season.

While many Germans became fans of the Dallas Mavericks during the era of German basketball icon Dirk Nowitzki, and interest in the Orlando Magic has been particularly high in recent years, that interest may spread in the coming season. A total of eight Germans are under contract on an NBA team for the 2026/27 season:

While Hartenstein, who won the NBA championship with the Thunder in 2025, has another shot at the title, Hukporti, now in Philadelphia, tore his Achilles tendon in the first preseason game and will be out for the entire season. The Sixers have signed NBA legend LeBron James and are considered one of the title contenders.

Maxi Kleber, a reliable bench player for the past nine years, did not receive a new contract from the Los Angeles Lakers and is currently a free agent.

The Charlotte Hornets could then become Germany's new favorite NBA team, with Germany captain and NBA nomad Dennis Schröder now on the roster. In his 14th year in the NBA, the Hornets are already his 12th different team.

Playing alongside him will be two German rookies, highly-touted Hannes Steinbach and Christian Anderson Jr. The two newcomers know each other from the German U19 national team, with which they won the silver medal at the 2025 World Championship.

"I'm a veteran — I've been in the league for 14 years now, I've actually been with the team the longest — and of course I'm trying to guide these two young guys through their rookie season and make it as easy as possible for them,” Schröder recently said in an interview with RTL/Sky Sport.

"It's really cool to have someone like that here. Dennis, of course, has already played a lot of games in the NBA," Steinbach said. "You have someone there you can speak German with, who gives you a few tips based on what he sees during the game."

The Hornets are aiming to make the playoffs at the end of the season. Since they play in the Eastern Conference, just like Brooklyn and Orlando, there will be plenty of matchups against the other German players along the way.

#993. Enzo Maresca addresses Gianluigi Donnarumma form after latest Man City blunder

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Donnarumma was at fault for one of the goals conceded in City’s 3-2 victory at RB Leipzig in the Champions League on Wednesday

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca insists Gianluigi Donnarumma has his full backing and is not concerned about the goalkeeper’s form.

Donnarumma was at fault for one of the goals conceded in City’s 3-2 victory at RB Leipzig in the Champions League on Wednesday when he allowed a shot to beat him at his near post.

There were also a couple of other uncomfortable moments for the Italy number one, who has made a number of uncharacteristic errors this season.

However, the former Paris Saint-Germain keeper did also make a fine save and Maresca is confident the 27-year-old will get back to his best.

Maresca said: “It’s not a concern, but it’s a mistake. We recognise that, he knows that it’s a mistake, but now it’s 48 hours (before) Nottingham Forest away, we need to be focused on that.”

Asked if he was thinking of reviewing the position during the upcoming international break, Maresca told reporters at a press conference: “I’m not, to be honest. Seriously, at the moment I’m not thinking about the international break and goalkeeper situation because we are talking about a mistake.

“A few minutes before the mistake he has made a save that any keeper in the world is not going to do. So it’s always a balance.

“Gigio knows that the first goal was not good but, again, he’s going to do better.”

Maresca accepts that his side needs to stop conceding “silly goals”.

City led twice through a Castello Lukeba own goal and Enzo Fernandez header but were pegged back by Ridle Baku and Antonio Nusa. They hit back again to win through Erling Haaland in the 78th minute.

Maresca said: “I think that both goals are quite silly goals that we can avoid.

“I think we are creating, since day one, many chances in each game but we need to avoid conceding silly goals.

“But I’m new here. I need to know the players, they need to know me. It’s four months that we are together.

“That’s why I’m so happy, so confident, because we can only improve after this short period.”

Maresca had warned before the game that his side could not only rely on Haaland to score their goals but the Norwegian was once again in the right place at the right time.

Haaland had been relatively quiet, touching the ball only 12 times before sliding on to Elliot Anderson’s perfectly-weighted through ball to settle the contest.

It was his 14th goal of the season and his 62nd in 61 career Champions League appearances. It was also his 176th for City, putting him within one of equalling Eric Brook as the club’s second-highest goalscorer.

Maresca said: “It’s always important that he’s in the game. We know that at any moment he can help us, he can score goals.

“We scored more goals with different players, and we created so many chances that unfortunately we missed, but again we’re happy with the three points because Champions League away in Germany is always difficult.”

#992. Cheaper cars are selling considerably faster than at the beginning of the year

Consumers are concerned about rising fuel prices and affordability — and that could be showing up in how fast the least expensive cars are moving off dealer lots.

From the first quarter to the third, the number of days it took a dealer to sell a vehicle priced between $20,000 and $29,999 dropped 20%, according to data from Edmunds. That pace of selling saw the biggest acceleration of any price segment.

Vehicles priced from $30,000 to $39,999 sold about 18% faster, and the number of days it took to sell the next tier — $40,000 to $49,999 — dropped nearly 12%, according to Edmunds.

All of those price segments also took fewer days to turn than their more expensive counterparts. The lower-priced tiers took under 60 days to move off lots, with the least expensive ones selling the fastest. Every segment of vehicles above $50,000, meanwhile, took more than 60 days to sell.

"If you're a dealer and you have inventory and that price point, you're definitely noticing," said Edmunds Director of Insights Ivan Drury.

Cheaper vehicles may be selling faster, but they're still hard to find. The average listing price for a new vehicle in September was $49,726, according to Cox Automotive.

And, the overall sales numbers for some key segments priced under $40,000 have fallen. This has especially been true for compact cars, which are down roughly 4% since the beginning of 2026, and compact SUVs, down nearly 8% in the same period, according to Cox Automotive.

These different data points seem to be moving in opposite directions. On the one hand, cheaper cars are moving faster off dealer lots. On the other, sales of affordable segments are down.

There are a few reasons for this, according to analysts who follow the industry. One is that there might not be enough lower-priced vehicles on dealer lots in the first place.

"I think there are some supply things going on at that end of the market," said Cox Automotive Deputy Chief Economist Mark Strand. "We have to kind of grade the market on a curve until we see what's going on with fourth-quarter data."

The compact SUV segment, in particular, is suffering from the lack of two popular models.

The Toyota RAV4, which is the most popular SUV in the U.S., has been in short supply at many dealerships this year, as the automaker shifts production to its Kentucky factory, Strand said. The company also has shifted the entire lineup to a hybrid powertrain at a time when hybrids have been in exceptionally high demand.

The other missing SUV is the Ford Escape, which that automaker discontinued to make way for its upcoming midsize EV pickup truck.

The other slow-selling, low-priced segment — compact cars — faces structural inventory challenges, said AutoForecast Solutions Vice President of Global Forecasting Sam Fiorani.

"We've seen the disappearance of affordable, compact new vehicles over the last decade," he said.

Detroit automakers swapped out their lineups of compact coupes and sedans in favor of small crossover SUVs, which tend to carry slightly higher sticker prices than comparably sized passenger cars.

Currently, there is not a single compact passenger sedan for sale by an American manufacturer. Most on the market are Japanese or Korean, with a few German models, such as the Volkswagen Jetta and the Golf hatchback.

"You have all these brands that have just abandoned the marketplace," Fiorani said.

The smallest American passenger cars are the Ford Mustang, General Motors' Chevrolet Corvette, and the midsize Tesla Model 3 sedan, according to AutoForecast Solutions. The firm classifies both the Mustang and the Corvette as sports cars, and as such they occupy a different niche than compact sedans like the Honda Civic or Toyota Corolla.

The Mustang has a starting price of $33,490, the Model 3 starts at $34,990 and the Chevrolet Corvette starts at $71,300. Cars like the Civic, Corolla and Jetta, meanwhile, all start below $25,000.

"Compact vehicle buyers are very price-sensitive," Fiorani said. "And so when the price of gas goes up, that eats into their car payment. That means that they can't afford a $500 or $600 a month car payment, and they have to move into the used market."

Indeed, the wholesale used prices of compact cars have risen and are up more than almost any other segment, according to Cox Automotive. Wholesale prices — the prices vehicles sell for at large auctions, like Cox Automotive's Manheim auction — are indicators for prices overall in the fragmented used-car market.

Along with the rise in prices, auto finance stats show that a historically high number of buyers are stretching to afford cars.

Roughly one in four buyers financing their purchases are getting 84-month loans — a record. Nearly 3 in 10 trade-ins toward new-vehicle purchases carried negative equity in the third quarter, meaning the cars being traded in were worth less than the outstanding balances of the loans on them. Shoppers are often rolling these negative balances into new loans, which pushes up the new payment cost.

Automakers have also been more tightly aligning production with demand to avoid discounting vehicles. Incentives on average are about 6.6% of the average transaction price as of October, according to Cox Automotive. Leasing offers a way to get a car with a lower payment, but leasing rates are also down.

Vehicle trade-in data suggests that many buyers who are snapping up those fast-selling cheaper vehicles are either first-time buyers or are purchasing supplemental vehicles, Edmunds' Drury said.

The subcompact SUV segment is one lower-priced group that has seen sales rise in 2026. That is a segment that attracts a lot of first-time buyers. But this is still a relatively small share of the total car market, Fiorani said.

"It's not the mainstream vehicle that Americans want," he said. "It is the vehicle that entry-level buyers need to get to work, to get to school. ... It's people who don't have families yet."

Repeat buyers are less likely to want to step down into a compact car or SUV, Drury said.

"The moment you get into that other vehicle and it's a little bit smaller, it's not as comfortable, it doesn't fit all your stuff, all your kid's equipment for soccer practice, you're done," he said. "You're not giving up 360 cameras, ventilated seats, heated steering wheels, these niceties that you've become accustomed to. Automakers know that too. Dealers know that."

The truly cash-strapped are either snapping up the relatively few low-priced cars on dealer lots, moving to the used market, or holding on to their cars longer.

"The people who are trying to buy the smaller vehicles are really hurt by the way the economy is at the moment," Fiorani said. "So those people are trying to move into used vehicles or trying to maintain their current vehicle as long as they can. Automakers should be prepared for a softening in the marketplace."

#990. Cristiano Ronaldo retires from international football

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Ronaldo calls time on his career with Portugal as international football’s all-time top scorer after a dispute with his country’s federation

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Cristiano Ronaldo has retired from international football.

Ronaldo, 41, calls time on his career with Portugal after a legendary 23-year stint, scoring 146 goals in 234 games to become international football’s all-time top scorer and appearance maker.

He captained his nation to their first ever major title at Euro 2016, while also lifting two Nations League titles in 2019 and 2025.

“The day has come back for me to hand back the number 7 shirt of our national team,” he said in an announcement on social video. “I never felt it belonged to me alone. But for 23 years I had the privilege and the responsibility of wearing it, defending it, and carrying it with me into stadiums all around the world.

“Today, the time has come to pass it on to the future. It was not an easy decision. Because some decisions are not made with the mind alone. They are also made with the heart.

“A journey that began in August 2003 and changed my life forever has come to an end. When I look back at everything with the national team, I don’t just see the matches, goals, records or trophies.

“I see people. I see the Portuguese people living abroad who, for 90 minutes, felt a little closer to home. I see millions of Portuguese people I have never met but who became part of my life. Because at the end of the day, football is so much bigger than a game. Football is about people.”

The five-time Ballon d’Or winner’s retirement follows his controversial decision to quit the Portugal camp during the international break last month, where he accused new manager Jorge Jesus of twice breaking his word after remaining an unused substitute against Norway.

The Portuguese FA handed Ronaldo a 30-day suspension - which would be served before the November international break - as well as imposing a €255 (£214.88) fine, with Jesus having not closed the door on bringing the country’s captain back into the fold.

However, Ronaldo has now taken the decision to permanently step away from Portugal duty, a month after storied rival Lionel Messi played his last game for Argentina.

Ronaldo made his Portugal debut in August 2003 when he came on as a half-time substitute for fellow legend Rui Costa in a 1-0 friendly win over Kazakhstan, eight days after completing his move from Sporting CP to Manchester United.

He scored his first goal at Euro 2004, bagging in a 2-1 group-stage loss to Greece, who Portugal would eventually lose to again in the final. He was named in the team of the tournament at 19.

Ronaldo was involved in an infamous incident with club team-mate Wayne Rooney in the Euro 2006 quarter-finals, with Ronaldo rushing over to the referee to protest after the Englishman was involved in a tangle with Ricardo Carvalho. Rooney was subsequently shown red, with Ronaldo caught winking on camera to add further fuel to the fire.

Ronaldo went on to appear at a joint-most six World Cup finals and an outright-most six European Championships, with his crowning glory coming in France in 2016.

Ronaldo’s best World Cup finish saw Portugal beaten in the semi-finals by France in 2006, with Zinedine Zidane’s penalty proving the difference in a 1-0 win.

His final attempt to claim a World Cup winners’ medal ended in tearful failure this year when Portugal were knocked out by eventual champions Spain in the last-16, courtesy of Mikel Merino’s stoppage-time winner.

“Throughout my entire career with the national team I always pushed myself beyond my limits,” he continued in his statement.

“I wanted to win, I wanted to be better, I wanted to make history. I always demanded the most of myself. I always wanted more. I always believed we could go further. And I gave everything I had for this shirt.

“There were perfect afternoons and nights. There were victories I will never forget. There were defeats that still hurt to remember.

“I made mistakes. I suffered. There were also moments when I couldn’t give the Portuguese people what they so desperately wanted. But I never gave up. And above all, I never stopped feeling proud to represent Portugal”

In a statement, the Portuguese Football Federation paid tribute to the country’s “eternal captain” and promised to organise an event in his honour.

“It is with a feeling of deep gratitude and immense admiration that the Portuguese Football Federation publicly praises and thanks Cristiano Ronaldo’s absolutely extraordinary career at the service of our country,” said the statement.

“Cristiano Ronaldo raised the name of Portugal and inspired generations of young people who dream of following in his footsteps, being for many of us, the best player of all time!

“Therefore, the Portuguese Football Federation refuses to let this goodbye be made without due tribute.

“It is our firm and enormous desire to organise, plan, participate and actively collaborate in what will always be a tribute to the height of Cristiano Ronaldo’s immense career, in which the fans and the country can applaud and celebrate, once again, the player who gave us so much.”

Ronaldo remains 15 strikes short of 1,000-goal target before he retires from football for good, with his only scoring avenue coming in Saudi Arabia with current club Al-Nassr.

#989. Germany news: Hackers release AfD party emails

Germany's far-right AfD has launched an inquiry after the release of thousands of emails following a cyberattack. Also, investors pledged billions for Germany at a major summit in Berlin. DW has more news from Germany.

This blog is now closed. Below is a round-up of top stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, October 20, 2026.

Alice Weidel, the co-leader of Germany's far-right AfD, is expected to present her party's policy for the EU at the European Parliament on Wednesday.

According to a report from news outlet Politico, the AfD policy paper on the EU does not seek to exit the bloc or the eurozone at first.

The party rather wants to downsize the EU's powers and budget.

Instead of direct European Parliament elections, the AfD would like to see delegates appointed by national parliaments. The AfD would also limit the scope of the European Commission to purely administrative tasks and supplant the European Court of Justice with an arbitration tribunal.

The AfD would threaten to slash Germany's contributions to the EU budget.

Germany under the AfD would seek exemptions from EU regulations regarding issues such as migration and social policy. The AfD may also seek opt-outs of other areas such as agriculture and financial policies.

If the EU would not bend to the AfD's demands for reform, the party would then seek a German referendum on EU membership.

A referendum would be unrealistic, as it would require a constitutional amendment to the German Basic Law to take place. An amendment would require a two-thirds majority vote in both the Bundestag and upper house Bundesrat — an extremely high threshold to meet.

The AfD hopes that it can implement its EU policies in 2029, when the next German and European elections will take place.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Recent German federal election surveys show the AfD in first place but it would have to form a coalition with another partner to establish a ruling majority government. That's difficult when other parties such as the conservative Christian Democratic Union refuse to have any cooperation with the AfD as part of a "firewall" policy.

More than 421,000 emails linked to Germany's far-right AfD have been published following a cyberattack (see additional entry below).

The alleged material includes private communications, sensitive personal data and reported references to racism, antisemitism and Nazi ideology, although much of the trove has not yet been independently verified.

Could this become one of the biggest political data leaks in modern German history?

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A German supermarket is getting attention online after responding to a customer who objected to its diverse workforce.

Nine pro-Palestinian protesters seeking an end to Western arms exports to Israel glued themselves to the ground in front of a Berlin facility belonging to German weapons manufacturer Rheinmetall.

Berlin police responded to the incident at 5:30 a.m. (0330 UTC) with 11 protesters at the site. The "Peacefully Against Genocide" group was behind the action.

The factory began arms production in June. It is involved in the production of shell casings for artillery ammunition and parts for kamikaze drones, according to local public broadcaster RBB.

It is unclear how much the facility in Berlin's Wedding neighborhood is involved with weapons for Israel. Rheinmetall, however, is Germany's largest arms manufacturer.

In the western German state of Hesse, seven people also blocked the entry to the Rheinmetall facility in the city of Kassel, according to local police.

In addition, demonstrators against weapons exports glued themselves in front of a weapons company in the western city of Kaiserslautern.

Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) said on Tuesday that it was looking into the theft and subsequent online publication of emails stolen by unidentified hackers during a cyberattack last month.

An AfD spokesperson said the hackers had targeted a hosting provider used by the party and appeared to have copied data from a small number of mostly inactive email accounts.

"The recent online publication of what is presumably a portion of this data is currently being investigated," the spokesperson said. "A preliminary assessment can only be provided once this investigation has been concluded."

Although the spokesperson did not say how much data was stolen, an earlier report by the mass-circulation daily Bild put the number of AfD-linked emails published at more than 420,000.

According to Bild, the material published included not only emails sent by party figures such as co-leader Alice Weidel but also bank statements, academic certificates and membership lists.

The website hosting the material was offline by Tuesday afternoon.

However, archived versions showed a volume of 281 gigabytes of data under the headline "The party's own records, unedited."

The emails and other materials published have not yet been certified as authentic by any independent body.

The AfD, several state chapters of which have been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by regional branches of Germany's domestic intelligence agency, has been topping recent national opinion polls and made gains in recent state elections.

Some politicians and civil society groups have called for it to be banned, arguing that the party is a threat to democracy, an accusation the party has rejected.

While Berlin hosts a summit on investment in Germany, an increasing amount of US capital is flowing into Germany's traditional industrial firms and family-owned businesses.

As many business owners struggle to find successors, more companies are becoming acquisition targets.

Read all the details here: Why US investors are snapping up Germany's famed Mittelstand

German economic confidence — like that across the eurozone in general — deteriorated in October, according to experts at the Mannheim-based Center for European Economic Research (ZEW).

The ZEW's monthly economic confidence index fell to a three-month low on Tuesday, down to 28.1 from 34.7 in September. That is nearly two points lower than forecast.

"Private consumption and investment remain weak because of high energy prices: They put real incomes under pressure, increase production costs and keep inflation higher for longer," said ZEW President Achim Wambach.

"The German economy," added Wambach, "is slowly emerging from stagnation, but the recovery is not self-sustaining."

The biggest losers in this latest index were banks, insurers, the service sector and the telecommunications industry.

Winners were seen in the metal manufacturing and electronics industries.

ZEW compiles its monthly surveys from interviews with banking, insurance and financial industry experts and businesses on their expectations for economic and capital market developments.

The ZEW's index is considered a key indicator for Germany's economic development.

Tuesday's survey was based on interviews with 178 analysts between October 12 and 19, 2026.

Chancellor Friedrich Merzhas indulged in an abundance of the most common cliches about his country and compatriots while trying to portray Germany as the ideal place to do business at an investment summit.

"Germans are hardworking, going to bed early, rising before dawn," he told the domestic and international guests at the Invest in Germany Summit.

"Worst traffic is in the morning between 6 and 7," he said.

"On holidays, we are first on the beach, spreading towels before breakfast. If we agree on delivery dates, we stick to it. If you invite friends from Germany for dinner at 7, we will arrive at 6:58.

"We are reliable, predictable, precise, and unsurprising," the chancellor continued. "We are, in short, what investors like most."

Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil also used blunt humor in his appeal to potential investors, saying in his speech simply: "I want your money."

Both pitches appear to have succeeded, with investment commitments worth billions made at the summit.

More than €225 billion ($252.5 billion) has so far been pledged in investments in Germany at a summit in Berlin attended by top business leaders, German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche said on Tuesday.

Reiche did not give any details about the commitments made so far, but told broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that the figure only included deals above a volume of €100 million.

Among those planning to invest in Europe's largest economy is online retail giant Amazon, which said it intended to pour some €16 billion into Germany next year for various schemes.

The company said these would include "the expansion of data centers and AI infrastructure, high-speed satellite internet through Amazon Leo, new logistics projects across the country, and a major new production slate by Prime Video."

"Germany is a hub of innovation and one of the most attractive investment opportunities in Europe," David Zapolsky, Amazon's chief global affairs and legal officer, was quoted as saying in a statement.

"That is why we have invested more than €100 billion here since 2010, and why we plan to invest an additional €16 billion in 2027. We want German businesses, communities, and creators to have the infrastructure and tools they need to compete and grow."

More than 200 German and international executives from large corporations, investment banks and funds are attending the gathering, entitled the Invest in Germany Summit.

The Left Party in Berlin, which has faced accusations of being antisemitic, is holding a meeting to discuss how to deal with its parliamentarian Vanessa Emde, who has raised controversy with pro-Palestinian statements.

Among other things, Emde has supported the idea that there is no right to exist for states, but only for people — thus seemingly going against Germany's firm support of Israel's right to existence.

Emde has refused to retract any of her statements.

She has also criticized a statement on antisemitism that she had signed along with all other members of the Left's parliamentary party in which the signatories committed to upholding Israel's right to existence.

This comes as both the Berlin Green Party and the Social Democrats (SPD) confirmed that they were ready to begin coalition negotiations with the Left Party on forming a joint government in the city-state.

The Left Party is due to decide on the issue on October 31 at a party conference.

The three parties held preliminary discussions on the accusations of antisemitism and links to organized crime leveled at the Left Party before beginning the exploratory talks that precede final coalition negotiations.

The Left Party emerged from September 20 elections in Berlin as the strongest party with 25.7% of the vote.

Both the Greens (14.3%) and the center-left SPD (12.1%) came in behind the conservative Christian Democrats (18.8%), who led a previous coalition in Berlin with the SPD.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) received 16.3% of the vote, but so far, all other parties are officially refusing to enter into any form of cooperation with it at either federal or state level.

The Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin entered its second and final day on Tuesday after opening the previous evening with a speech by Chancellor Friedrich Merz that included the words: "Germany is open for business."

The summit has already yielded an agreement to deepen cooperation on artificial intelligence (AI) in German industry between Germany and US tech giant Nvidia.

Merz and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the combination of Germany's engineering expertise and cutting-edge AI technology would help strengthen the country's economy over the long term.

More than 200 German and international executives representing large corporations, investment banks and funds are attending the event, with closed-door talks scheduled for Tuesday.

The summit aims to attract foreign investment to Germany. Organizers highlight the country's sound public finances, triple-A credit rating as the only G7 nation to hold one, strong rule of law and leading position in European patent filings.

Despite these advantages, Germany has struggled to attract foreign investment in recent years, with high energy prices and labor costs acting as deterrents.

Government sources say investment will be vital to help bridge gaps in public funding as the country seeks to improve infrastructure and support companies' transition to climate-neutral production.

The summit is also being attended by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, who also serves as Merz's deputy.

Nine protesters have glued themselves to the road outside a plant run by defense contractor Rheinmetall in Berlin's Wedding district, police said on Tuesday.

Officers have been trying since the early morning to detach the group, a police spokeswoman said.

She said as many as 90 officers had been deployed to the site, where altogether 11 protesters were gathered.

Rheinmetall is Germany's largest weapons manufacturer.

The plant in Wedding, where production began earlier this year, has been the target of several protests, with climate and social justice activist Greta Thunberg among those participating.

German industrial giant Siemens has warned against eliminating entry-level jobs that are now increasingly left to artificial intelligence (AI), saying young workers could be left without essential skills, including those needed to monitor AI-generated work.

Judith Wiese, the company's chief people and sustainability officer, said that handing certain routine tasks to AI meant that young employees would not gain hands-on experience that could benefit them later in their careers.

Wiese said it was necessary, for example, for software developers to be able to write their own code so they could critically examine the code produced by AI.

"The crucial question is always: What do I need to have done, checked and seen myself to avoid being misled by AI?" she said.

However, Wiese said AI could also help employees acquire skills more quickly, while older colleagues could learn from younger ones who had grown up using AI.

Wiese said it was still too early to say how AI would impact employment.

Noting that Siemens has some 30,000 software engineers, she said: "You can use the additional productivity either to do the same work with fewer people or to do more with the same number of employees."

Wiese also pointed out that AI was speeding up work processes, enabling the exploration of new ideas and creating projects that would not have been possible without it.

DW''s newsroom in Bonn bids a warm guten Tag to all its readers as a previously balmy October decides to move toward more wintry chill.

As Chancellor Merz hosts an investment conference in Berlin where developments in AI is taking center stage, industrial giant Siemens has warned that the technology does not only bring advantages.

The controversy over alleged antisemitism in Berlin's Left Party, which might well soon lead a leftist coalition in the city-state, continues, with the party itself debating what to do about a member who has expressed strong anti-Israel views.

And people in Germany are likely to face much longer waits for doctors' appointments from next year, according to an organization managing family doctors and therapists across Germany.

Liverpool star Rio Ngumoha could become the next Red to head to Bayern Munich, with Die Roten eyeing up the star.

The 18-year-old has been fantastic since moving to Anfield at the start of last year, forcing his way into the plans of Arne Slot before the Dutchman was replaced by Andoni Iraola at the start of this season.

But Liverpool may well have shot themselves in the foot when it comes to keeping Ngumoha – thanks to another big-money move they made over the summer.

Liverpool sold Luis Diaz to Bayern Munich last summer, and have been busy investing in talents able to play on the left wing position ever since.

Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Hugo Ekitike can all play there – along with Ngumoha, and new signings Victor Munoz and Bradley Barcola.

Now, BILD in Germany has reported that Bayern are eyeing Ngumoha as competition for Diaz, after losing out on signing Barcola.

The Bavarians were reportedly keen on signing the Frenchman but were put off by the fee that Paris Saint-Germain were demanding over the summer, with The Athletic reporting that Barcola signed for the Reds for a whopping £106 million, with £17m in potential add-ons.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Since opting not to sign anyone, Vincent Kompany's side have lost the likes of Diaz, Serge Gnabry and Jamal Musiala to injury, which left Alphonso Davies as the starting left-winger against Arsenal in the Champions League two weeks ago.

Ngumoha would be considerably cheaper than Barcola was, and would follow the same pattern that Bayern followed when signing Musiala.

After the likes of Jadon Sancho and Jude Bellingham blazed a trail by going to the Bundesliga as teenagers to play competitive first-team football, Bayern convinced Stuttgart-born, London-raised Musiala to follow at the age of 16.

Musiala later switched allegiance from England to Germany internationally and has taken the No.10 shirt for club and country.

While Ngumoha has had plenty of first-team action on Merseyside already for his young age, Bayern are said to want to want to strengthen as soon as January to address their current injury crisis – leaving the England international with a major decision to make about the pathway he has under Iraola.

Ngumoha is worth €50m, according to Transfermarkt. Liverpool travel to Fenerbahce as Champions League action resumes tonight.

#987. Automakers like Rivian and Ford are ‘democratizing 3D printing’ to reduce costs and increase speed

DETROIT — Automakers including Ford Motor and Rivian Automotive are leaning into a new type of manufacturing line: 3D printing.

Manufacturers say it's helping them reduce costs and increase speed. The technology has been around for decades, but it's becoming more commoditized in the automotive industry, with 3D printers used to create everything from vehicle parts and accessories to tools for assembly plants and testing units for research and development labs.

"At this point, we don't have a choice but to scale up and begin using it through all factions of Rivian," Jonathan Dankenbring, Rivian senior manager of prototype manufacturing, told CNBC during a tour of the automaker's expansive 3D-printing operations in suburban Detroit. "We're going to be democratizing 3D printing for the entire company."

Also known as additive manufacturing, 3D printing can create three-dimensional objects from digital designs by dispensing material layer by layer, much like a traditional printer does with ink on paper. Instead of ink, the machines use a wide variety of materials such as plastics, composites, ceramics and even metals.

Printers can range from hundreds of dollars for hobby-like devices to hundreds of thousands of dollars for specialty equipment, depending on how big the product being produced is and the material it needs. They can produce individual pieces or hundreds of smaller parts in a batch using powders and resins.

Rivian said it has spent more than $5 million on 3D-printing machines, with the cost of materials for the operations growing to about $1.7 million annually.

Dankenbring said despite the costs, the machines typically pay for themselves within a year. He said the technology helps lower supplier tooling costs, streamline logistics expenses and cut production times for parts from weeks to days, if not hours.

"It's well in the millions [for savings], but the main thing is speed for Rivian," Dankenbring said.

The all-electric vehicle company's latest expansion of 3D printing includes adding new machines that can build flexible silicone parts as well as installing a bay of machines at its plant in Normal, Illinois, for employees to print parts on demand.

"3D prints should be readily available for every engineer so that they can make a part and get it in their hands as soon as possible," Dankenbring said.

Rivian has also used the technology for electric-motor models for fluid testing, creating screw guides for tooling and stamping press inserts and some production parts, including trim pieces to fill gaps in some early builds.

There's a similar push underway at larger, more-established automakers like Ford and its crosstown rival General Motors, which have used 3D printing for many years, including in their massive assembly plants.

Instead of having a bay of 3D-printing machines like at Rivian, Ford has departments for additive manufacturing at many of its plants to produce and distribute needed parts. That includes a new vending machine for 3D-printed parts for production of F-150 pickup trucks near its Dearborn, Michigan, headquarters.

"By putting the vending machine up, all the team leaders have access," said Gregory Foresi, a Ford mechanical engineer who ran Ford's 3D-printing lab at the plant from 2024 until last month. "We're able to keep that thing stocked rather than have a bunch of parts laying around in the lab. So that's been pretty huge."

Foresi used roughly two dozen machines to print off thousands of tools, some of which have been designed by employees, such as torque bit sockets, hood jackers and hand tools for smoothing adhesive.

Employees can use an app to request that specific auto parts or tools be printed. Ford's 3D-printing teams help develop them or determine what to produce next, as the machining time to build different parts can range from hours to days, if not weeks.

Foresi said creating the tools with 3D printing has allowed the automaker to uniquely design them when needed, get them faster and, in many cases, receive them at a lower cost.

Ford also has used 3D-printed parts to help keep production running. For example, Foresi said a large machining wheel was needed to maintain assembly line production and the company was able to 3D print the part until a permanent replacement from a supplier was available.

"They didn't perform as well, and it's not really a replacement for the ones that we were purchasing, but they kept the plant running," Foresi said.

Ford said it expects to have 3D labs deployed at more than 23 plants by the end of this year. Its current 3D-printing program has more than 200 machines, and there are additional printers outside the official program, the company said.

GM has used 3D-printed parts for some of its low-volume products in addition to research and development and inside plants, including recently expanding its use of industrial Stratasys printers that can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars based on use case, training and certification.

The Detroit automaker uses 135 components that are 3D-printed for its bespoke Cadillac Celestiq as well as other components for its performance Cadillac Blackwing sedans, including a unique medallion on the manual shifter knob.

Fadi Abro, senior global director of automotive and mobility at 3D-printing company Stratasys, said GM has been a great example of how companies can "standardize and then scale" 3D printing.

"The material properties improved so significantly that the use cases improved," he said, noting the company works with virtually every major automaker. "From a product perspective, we have to get the technology to become faster and more accessible, in an economic sense."

Correction: This story has been updated to reflect that Jonathan Dankenbring is Rivian's senior manager of prototype manufacturing. A previous version of this article misidentified him.

Could Manchester United legend David Beckham save the club from the Glazers?

Manchester United legend David Beckham has been named as a potential buyer to turn the Red Devils' fortunes around.

Man United won just their third match of the season last night at home to Roma in the Champions League, sparking a miraculous recovery from 2-0 down to beat the side from the Eternal City 3-2 in the dying embers of the game.

But despite this, the future of the club remains unclear, with manager Michael Carrick still in danger of being sacked and opinion of the Old Trafford ownership at rock bottom following an appalling start to the season.

In 2024, INEOS CEO Jim Ratcliffe became a minority shareholder in his boyhood club, taking control of sporting operations away from the much-despised Glazer family, who had run United since assuming full control of the club back in 2005.

Ratcliffe's tenure as owner has been troubling, too, however, with United on their third manager in as many years and a lack of investment criticised by the fans – while the Monaco-based billionaire's comments on immigrants and his decisions to make wide-scale redundancies at United have been met with widespread condemnation.

Speaking on a recent episode of The Good, The Bad and The Football, sponsored by Midnite. United legend Paul Scholes was asked about the prospect of former team-mate David Beckham taking over the club, and greeted the proposition openly.

Scholes is a co-owner of Salford City with Beckham as one of the Project 92 Limited group, with the latter also involved as an owner of Inter Miami in Major League Soccer.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“I don’t see why not, if they’ve got the wealth to do it,” Scholes responded when prompted by presenter Paddy McGuinness over whether Beckham could take over United.

These owners haven’t worked, and I know Jim Ratcliffe’s only been there for two and a half years, but it just hasn’t worked so far, has it?

“We all know what the feeling around the club is about the Glazers, so I’d be open to anybody.”

Co-star Nicky Butt, meanwhile, was a little more cautious when asked about a potential takeover, noting that the Glazer family value the club at £8 billion.

“The biggest problem you’ve got is the Glazers will want a piece of the pie,” he added.

The Beckhams are worth around £1.1bn, as relayed by the BBC. United host Aston Villa this weekend as Premier League action continues.

#985. Seamus Coleman takes on new Republic of Ireland role as Everton legend ponders his playing future

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Seamus Coleman has not played since leaving Everton at the end of last season

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Seamus Coleman has been handed a fresh role within the Republic of Ireland set-up by manager Heimir Hallgrimsson, who wants to help extend the veteran defender's playing career.

The former Ireland captain has been drafted in as part of a new ‘hybrid role’.

Coleman, 38, has been a free agent since his departure from Everton at the end of last season. He has spoken openly about the possibility of retiring from the game.

Hallgrimsson named a 24-man squad for this month's Nations League fixtures against Austria and Kosovo, and Coleman's name was not on the list.

But the manager went out of his way to announce that the full-back would be joining up with the group. Coleman will work alongside the management group during the camp.

He will also take part in some of the team's training sessions, which keeps alive the possibility of adding to his 81 international caps.

“I can inform you that Seamus will be in some sort of a hybrid role this camp. He is going to do the sessions with the players, but he is going to be in a leadership role and supportive role with us as coaches,” explained Hallgrimsson.

“Hopefully that will get him to start playing again. That’s our aim, to try to push him to continue playing. He has expressed that he wants to do that. We need to see where he is at. He hasn’t done team training for some period now, so we need to see where he is at.

“Obviously it’s tempting (to call him up) with how he did for us without playing much for Everton. It makes us believe that he can always play for the national team and do good. But we will have to wait and see.”

There were few surprises elsewhere in the squad. Fit-again skipper Nathan Collins returns, along with Harvey Vale and goalkeeper Mark Travers.

Ireland travel to Linz on November 14. They then host Kosovo in Dublin three days later.

Two wins from those games could see them promoted to League A. A single point may be enough to secure a play-off spot as they look to position themselves for European Championship qualification.

Josh Cullen was not called on by Hallgrimsson. The Burnley midfielder has only recently returned from a lengthy lay-off, and the manager is instead allowing him to build his readiness before adding to his workload.

“I spoke to Josh in London, he’s very close to fitness but maybe not international fitness. Not a 90-minute fitness,” he said. “He wants to wait and fully get his fitness back with staff at his club.”

The fixtures also come too soon for Evan Ferguson and Jaden Umeh, who are each working their way back from injuries.

Hallgrimsson was more guarded on the subject of Shea Lacey. The Manchester United prospect is a Liverpool-born England youth international who could qualify for Ireland through his father.

Asked whether he had made any contact to check on the 19-year-old's interest, he said: “Not from me, that would be for other guys within the association to have that contact. It was interesting, looking at his Irish connection…interesting.”

#984. Baked by Melissa enters Target with first at-home cupcake mix

Baked by Melissa will enter the at-home baking aisle in Target stores as the retailer tries to persuade shoppers to spend more at its locations this holiday season.

As of Sunday, Target is exclusively selling the brand's cupcake kits, liners and a cupcake pan, all in the dessert company's signature bite-size portions. The line includes three cupcake flavors: Christmas Tie-Dye, Marshmallow Hot Cocoa and Red Velvet.

The company's entry into at-home baking comes as a number of restaurants turn to consumer packaged goods to boost sales in an otherwise challenging time for the industry.

Some players, such as California Pizza Kitchen and TGI Fridays, have licensed their brands for frozen foods for decades. But other restaurant chains, including Chick-fil-A and Dutch Bros, have leaned into grocery products much more recently. For smaller companies, such as Momofuku or Carbone, space on a grocery shelf helps extend brand reach and gives consumers a chance to try their food without a reservation and at a much lower cost.

Founded by Melissa Ben-Ishay in 2008, Baked by Melissa has nine permanent locations in the New York area and ships its minicupcakes nationwide.

The regional chain has garnered attention outside the city thanks to Ben-Ishay's social media presence. On TikTok, the Baked by Melissa account has more than 2.8 million followers, fueled by popular recipe videos, such as for her green goddess salad dressing. Ben-Ishay's social media stardom has led to collaborations with Ferrero and Wonder.

Baked by Melissa had discussed at-home baking products for years, but Ben-Ishay, who is also president of the company, only decided to take the plunge a year ago during a trip to Target with her two kids, she told CNBC. A spin through the baking aisle made her decide Baked by Melissa "should be here," she said.

"I love baking cake mix. I truly do. And, quite frankly, sometimes I just think it tastes better," Ben-Ishay said.

But retail moves more slowly than Baked by Melissa's usual pace.

The dessert company needed just a few days to create New York Knicks-branded minicupcakes after the team won the NBA championship in June, for example, but figuring out retail products meant "a lot of waiting and approvals and new partners," Ben-Ishay said.

Twelve months later, the cupcake mixes have arrived on store shelves, just in time for the all-important holiday season.

For Target, the next two months will be critical as the retailer tries to woo back its core customer after a disappointing holiday season last year. That prototypical Target shopper often looks a lot like Ben-Ishay.

"We started with Target because I'm a 42-year-old mom of two, and I find myself there a lot," she said.

#983. Epileptic seizures nearly vanish after people receive experimental gene therapy in their brains

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Mariana Lenharo is a reporter for Nature in New York City.

A scan shows the brain of a man with epilepsy. A newly developed gene therapy targets locations in the brain that are the root of epileptic seizures. Credit: Allison Robbert/The Washington Post/Getty

Three people with epilepsy resistant to drug treatment saw the number of seizures they had per month fall by more than 90%, after gene-laden viruses were infused directly into their brains as part of an early-stage clinical trial1.

In each participant, the gene therapy was precisely targeted to a small patch of brain tissue that was the source of their seizures. The viruses carried a gene that makes neurons sensitive to a specific drug, which works like a dimmer switch for the therapy. By combining gene therapy with a drug — an approach known as chemogenetics — researchers can adjust a treatment’s potency, which is not possible with other types of gene therapy. The trial participants did not experience serious side effects.

Genetic therapies offer new hope against incurable brain diseases

Genetic therapies offer new hope against incurable brain diseases

The results were reported today in The New England Journal of Medicine by Yang Dai, a neurosurgeon at Xuanwu Hospital of Capital Medical University in Beijing, and his colleagues. “It’s exciting that there’s such a dramatic effect, and that they see very few side effects,” says Matthew Walker, a neurologist at University College London who was not associated with the study.

But he cautions that the study is small. He is also concerned about the long-term use of the drug that participants took after receiving the gene therapy. High doses of the drug, an anti-psychotic called clozapine, have been associated with cardiovascular problems and other negative effects. “In the future, hopefully there are going to be better drugs” for this form of treatment, says Walker, who is the co-founder of the start-up company Focalis Bio in Canterbury, UK, which is also developing gene therapies for epilepsy.

The three trial participants were adults with a common form of epilepsy caused by hippocampal sclerosis, a type of scarring in a region of the brain called the hippocampus. The participants had this scarring on only one side of the hippocampus. All three had been diagnosed with epilepsy 10–25 years earlier and had developed resistance to at least two anti-seizure drugs. They also had at least two seizure episodes per month, on average, over the three months before they enrolled in the trial.

The experimental treatment uses a virus called adeno-associated virus 9 to deliver a gene to neurons in the affected area. The gene was engineered to produce proteins specifically in excitatory cells — the ones that are involved in seizures.

Brain editing now ‘closer to reality’: the gene-altering tools tackling deadly disorders

Brain editing now ‘closer to reality’: the gene-altering tools tackling deadly disorders

The gene instructs neurons to produce a receptor that binds to clozapine. Clozapine acts like a switch and activates these receptors, reducing the activity of the targeted neurons, the authors say. That reduced activity helps to suppress the abnormal electrical activity that triggers seizures.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03566-2

Dai, Y. et al. N. Engl. J. Med. 395, 1867–1869 (2026).

Aston Villa manager Unai Emery has rebuilt the Midlands outfit, and has his team looking steady on all fronts after a crazy summer.

After winning the Europa League, the Basque boss saw the spine of his side ripped out, with Emiliano Martinez, Ezri Konsa, Lucas Digne, Youri Tielemans, Morgan Rogers and Ollie Watkins all sold – and Aston Villa started the season understandably poorly as a result.

#981. Cristiano Ronaldo’s long Portugal goodbye leaves complicated legacy

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Ronaldo was talismanically brilliant for Portugal and led them to Euro 2016 glory, but as Richard Jolly explains, he became a burden in his final few years, leaving plenty relieved by his international retirement

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

It could be called the long goodbye, although really it was an extremely long goodbye. The beginning of the end came in Qatar, in December 2022, when Portugal beat Switzerland 6-1, with a Goncalo Ramos hat-trick. Cristiano Ronaldo took almost four years to take a hint.

His retirement from international football came three months before his 42nd birthday, more than 23 years after his debut and two major tournaments too late. The undignified finish felt sadly inevitable. There was to be no happy ending: not when Portugal’s chances of winning Euro 2024 or the 2026 World Cup were fatally wounded by picking Ronaldo.

So instead the world’s second oldest toddler – it has not been a good week for ageing egomaniacs on either side of the Atlantic – ended up bidding farewell to his country by flouncing out of the camp last month after being left an unused substitute against Norway, wanting manager Jorge Jesus to apologise for “putting someone of the stature of Pele or Maradona on to warm up and then not putting him in the game”, in his own words, posting a self-pitying, self-important 2,000-word opus on Instagram. Ronaldo’s 30-day suspension from the Portuguese FA is as irrelevant as the much-mocked £215 fine; the real punishment for a billionaire is the eventual recognition that he cannot carry on for Portugal forever.

And the final chapter should not obscure what an astonishing career it has been. The numbers are beefed up by the last four years, but Ronaldo’s 234 caps and 146 goals are records in international football, and should remain so for quite some time. Astonishingly, he is 99 goals clear of Portugal’s second top scorer, Pauleta. Between them, Luis Figo and Eusebio scored half as many goals for their country as he did. For a long time, Eusebio’s status as Portugal’s greatest footballer went unchallenged. Now it is clear he stands in second place.

The last four years mean some of the statistics need qualifying. Ronaldo is Portugal’s record scorer in world cups, but it was only in the sixth that he passed Eusebio, who played in one. He is the only man to score in six World Cups, but the fact that only one of those goals came in a knockout game, and that was a penalty in a last-32 match, means he underwhelmed on the global stage.

Yet he can nevertheless be called the greatest player in the history of the European Championships; with 30 appearances and 14 goals. He is the only Portugal captain to lift a major trophy, and while he went off injured in the final of Euro 2016, the sight of Ronaldo on the sidelines, part coach, part super-fan, is one of the indelible images of his two decades of international football.

Perceptions of Portugal have been transformed in part by Ronaldo; until the generation of Figo and Rui Costa, 1966 was the great anomaly, the time Eusebio powered them to a World Cup semi-final the exception for a country that rarely qualified for anything. If Ronaldo’s best tournaments included his first two, in 2004 and 2006, when the core of a team was an older generation, he gave them a level of consistency and competitiveness.

There were two remarkable hat-tricks: one against Sweden to ensure they qualified for the 2014 World Cup, another against Spain in the 2018 tournament. There was also Ronaldo’s remarkable transformation from flair player to finisher. He scored 19 times in his first 50 caps, 37 times in his first 100: very good by anyone else’s standards, but he was only warming up. He scored 109 international goals after his 28th birthday.

His 146th and last strike for Portugal was the penalty against Croatia in Toronto. By then, however, Ronaldo had descended into selfishness and self-parody. In the 2022 World Cup, he tried to claim a goal Bruno Fernandes scored. In his last three major tournaments, his only goals in open play in 15 matches came against Uzbekistan.

He was arguably the worst player in Euro 2024; ineffective, immobile and, when Portugal had such talent on the bench, weakening the side. Yet he played 486 minutes out of a possible 510, the most of any outfield player. He was little better in the 2026 World Cup, but played 441 minutes out of 450.

His unholy alliance with Roberto Martinez may have been a feat of diplomacy from the Spaniard, but it became ever harder to deny that it damaged Portugal. Even when Ronaldo should have been ruled out, he was somehow reprieved in a way that seemed to suit Gianni Infantino and Donald Trump: rather than being suspended for the start of the World Cup after his red card against Ireland, the last three games of his ban magically disappeared.

Ronaldo, it seemed, got preferential treatment from his manager and the governing bodies.

A talented Portugal team suffered, impotent when it mattered, hampered by a statuesque centre-forward. Seemingly starstruck, they sacrificed some of the prime years of Fernandes, Bernardo Silva, Ruben Dias and many others. They sacrificed Ramos, benched when it was evident the team was better with him in it.

Yet still Ronaldo carried on after the World Cup. Perhaps it took Jesus, a blunter figure than Martinez, to end the madness of it all. As Ronaldo’s Portugal career is finally over, he has many a tribute, but his manager and teammates could be forgiven for feeling a sense of relief.

Manchester United director of football Jason Wilcox has come under fresh scrutiny following a new revelation about one of his preferred managerial targets

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Just when Manchester United supporters thought the club's decision-making couldn't appear any more disjointed, a revelation has laid bare the apparent lack of footballing acumen inside Old Trafford.

Hindsight is a wonderful thing, especially in football, but according to a report by The Athletic, prior to the 2024 FA Cup final against Manchester City, director of football Jason Wilcox championed Russell Martin as a serious candidate to replace the embattled Erik ten Hag.

It was a time when the club required a proven manager to arrest their slump which had crept in during the late-stage Ten Hag era. Fortunately, Wilcox’s suggested solution was deemed too parochial, even if the club did end up appointing Ruben Amorim whose tenure was short-lived.

The newly-installed INEOS hierarchy was conducting an exhaustive review into Ten Hag’s stewardship in the summer of 2024, actively vetting prospective managers.

Among the names put forward, Wilcox pushed Martin’s, seemingly drawing heavily on their close professional relationship.

It was Wilcox who had hired Martin at Southampton in the summer of 2023 during his brief stint as the Saints' director of football. While Martin did steer Southampton back to the Premier League via the Championship play-offs in May 2024, the idea that he was equipped to lead English football's biggest institution was a hard case to make.

The trajectory of Martin’s career since that 2024 Wembley triumph demonstrates just how disastrous that appointment could have been.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Upon arriving in the Premier League, Martin’s dogmatic approach to slow-tempo possession football unravelled in historic fashion. His Southampton side became notorious for defensive errors, giving up possession inside and around their own penalty area while shipping goals at an alarming rate.

Martin's apparent refusal to adapt or compromise his footballing ideology led to him developing a reputation as an obstinate idealist not equipped for a top-flight survival fight, or perhaps even top level management, let alone the hot seat at Old Trafford.

Man United ultimately opted for Amorim to succeed Ten Hag in November 2024. And while his reign was turbulent, handing the reins to Martin might have been even worse.

For all the flaws Amorim's side displayed on his watch, Martin’s insistence on playing out from deep with an already psychologically fragile defence would most likely have seen Man United dismantled by superior opposition.

The timing of this revelation lands at an inopportune time for Wilcox’s personal credibility. The former Manchester City executive was brought to Carrington by Sir Jim Ratcliffe to deliver a modern, data-driven football structure, but now Wilcox is facing accusations that he is out of his depth.

Pushing his former Southampton colleague forward for one of the most demanding managerial posts in world football doesn't chime with the kind of best-in-class mentality Man United seek. It has, at the very least, exposed a lack of imagination from an executive tasked with restoring a giant club to the summit of European football.

Presently, Michael Carrick clings to the top job on a temporary stay of execution, recruitment chief Christopher Vivell is being courted by Bayern Munich, and the dressing room remains fractured, despite Tuesday night's spirited fightback against AS Roma in the Champions League.

The club are not out of the woods just yet and with a fresh managerial appointment expected in the coming weeks, it could be the most important decision of Wilcox's tenure.

#979. FA and WSL announce investigation into ACL injuries in women's football

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

A number of high-profile players including Leah Williamson and Beth Mead have ruptured their ACLs in recent years

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A new research project will investigate anterior cruciate ligament injuries in women's football, after a series of high-profile players suffered ruptured anterior cruciate ligaments (ACL) in recent years.

The Football Association and the Women's Super League (WSL) have announced the study, which aims to better understand why the injuries occur and how incidences could be reduced.

Alexia Putellas, Sam Kerr, Beth Mead, Vivianne Miedema and Leah Williamson are among the players to have ruptured their ACLs in recent years.

Previous research has suggested female players are more at risk of the injury than their male counterparts.

The project is a collaboration with Imperial College London and knee surgeon Simon Ball. Sponsored by the FA, the PhD research will be carried out by Hanna Lehtovirta at Imperial College.

It will combine scientific data with the experiences of players and staff working in the professional game, and every club in the WSL and WSL2 will be invited to take part.

Data will be compared from players who have suffered ACL injuries and those who have not. Interviews with players will also form part of the research.

The ACL is one of the four main ligaments in the knee joint, and rupturing it is considered to be one of the most significant injuries in football, with players typically taking at least 6-9 months to recover from them before returning to the pitch.

Some of the most high-profile players in the women’s game have missed major tournaments because of the injury.

Williamson, who led England to Euros glory in 2022 and 2025, missed the 2023 World Cup after rupturing her ACL just weeks before the tournament. The Lionesses went on to reach the final in Australia without her before losing to Spain.

Putellas also had to battle back from the same injury, but proved she can still operate at the highest level by winning the women’s Ballon d’Or for the third time last week.

She also claimed the coveted prize in 2021 and 2022 during her time at Barcelona. Putellas left the Catalan giants earlier this year to join London City Lionesses in the WSL.

#978. Ferrari raises 2026 guidance after Q3 earnings beat

Ferrari on Tuesday raised its 2026 guidance after the sports car maker slightly beat Wall Street's third-quarter expectations.

Here's how Ferrari performed in the third quarter compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:

Ferrari raised its guidance to revenue of 7.65 billion euros, up from 7.6 billion euros; adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization to 3 billion euros, up from 2.97 billion euros; and adjusted EPS to at least 9.85 euros, up from at least 9.68 euros.

The automaker also upgraded its expectations for industrial free cash flow to up to 1.65 billion euros, up from previous expectations for at least 1.55 billion euros.

This is the second consecutive quarter Ferrari has raised its 2026 guidance, despite vehicle shipments being lower by 318 units through the first nine months of the year, at 10,170 vehicles, compared with last year. The decline is led by fewer shipments to the Americas and China, Hong Kong and Taiwan.

Ferrari said Tuesday that the guidance improvements were a result of stronger-than-expected customer personalizations, lower than anticipated currency headwinds and a second place finish in the Formula 1 championship.

"Our order book now reaches into 2028, and we still have two more launches to come this year. In addition, we continue to create engaging events around the world to further tighten the bonds with our clients and partners across Racing, Sports Cars and Lifestyle," Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna said in a release.

RBC Capital Markets analyst Tom Narayan said Tuesday that Ferrari's results were largely in line with Wall Street expectations. However, he said shares may be "under slight pressure given some were hoping for a bigger guidance raise, but expect it to get better once folks realize these results are healthy."

Ferrari's U.S. stock initially declined on the results before turning positive to close Tuesday at $414.77 a share, up 2.9%.
